title: What Happens When a Continuous Improvement Project Doesn’t Go as Planned?
summary: When most people think about continuous improvement, they picture successful projects and breakthrough ideas or measurable results.
body_markdown:
#


**By Mike Schnee, Sr. Director NGS**


When most people think about continuous improvement, they picture successful projects and breakthrough ideas or measurable results.


What they don’t always see is the learning that happens when the first solution falls short.


In my experience, that’s often where the most valuable improvement begins.


Each year, our President’s Week Kaizen events challenge teams to tackle important business opportunities that support customer success and operational excellence, along with long-term growth. These are not small process tweaks. They’re significant initiatives intended to help teams achieve meaningful business outcomes.


While many projects achieve their goals exactly as planned, others reveal something equally valuable: the need to adapt.


That’s where continuous improvement separates itself from traditional project management.


Continuous improvement isn’t about stubbornly following a plan because it was the original plan. It’s about evaluating results and learning from experience, making better decisions based on new information.


When teams reach the end of a sustainment period and haven’t achieved the outcomes they expected, I encourage them to ask a simple question: **What should we do differently?**


Sometimes the answer is new technology. Sometimes it’s additional collaboration. Sometimes it’s admitting that part of the original process wasn’t designed well enough and needs to be rethought entirely.


Those aren’t signs of failure. They’re signs that people are paying attention to what the data and the business are telling them.


One of the biggest mistakes organizations can make is continuing to repeat the same actions while expecting different results. True continuous improvement requires both persistence and adaptability.


The most successful improvement efforts share that mindset. Rather than accepting incomplete results or abandoning important goals, teams reassess their approach, engage additional partners, and explore new solutions.


Progress doesn’t always happen in a straight line.


Meaningful improvement requires teams to learn, adjust, and keep moving forward.


That’s why I often remind teams that continuous improvement is not about getting everything right on the first try.


It’s about creating an environment where employees are willing to learn from experience and try something better the next time.


Across every organization, the teams that achieve lasting improvements tend to share common characteristics:[collaboration, humility, innovation, and persistence](https://novanta.com/careers-culture/life-at-novanta/) . Those qualities allow setbacks to become opportunities for growth rather than reasons to stop.


Those same qualities are reflected in[The Novanta Way](https://novanta.com/about/) . When employees challenge existing processes, seek out new perspectives, collaborate across teams, and remain committed to delivering results, they’re demonstrating the mindset required for both continuous improvement and long-term business success.


The true measure of continuous improvement isn’t whether the first plan succeeds.


It’s whether you’re willing to learn from the outcome and adjust your approach all while continuing to work toward a better result.
